clue.text: Police place blundering Prince before court

indicators.note: something done blunderingly is botched and jumbled, so the word beside it is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
CT is the standard abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A clumsy royal is hauled to the police station before his court appearance.
explanation.definitionFit: A precinct is a district under one police station, and in American usage the station house itself.

clue.text: Oliver's requests for more?

blocks.note: surface reading: the orphan in Dickens holding out his bowl and asking for more gruel
setter's reading: in pontoon or blackjack a player asks the dealer for another card using a word that is also Oliver's surname

explanation.surface: Oliver Twist famously asks the workhouse master for more.
explanation.walkthrough: In card games like pontoon, saying TWIST asks for another card, and Oliver's surname is Twist, so his requests for more are TWISTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Players in pontoon call for an extra card with that word, so the plural names several such calls for more cards.

clue.text: Take away display on wall in quiet road

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside it

blocks.note: the hushing sound asking for quiet
to put a picture up on a wall
the A1, Britain's great north road, written as AI

explanation.surface: Someone is told to remove a wall display on a quiet street.
explanation.walkthrough: The A1 is the main road from London to Edinburgh, and crosswords write it with the letter I standing in for the digit 1.
explanation.definitionFit: To shanghai a person is to kidnap them, originally forcing sailors onto ships, so it means to carry off by force.

clue.text: Former captain dismissing Australia's openers for English to create pressure

indicators.note: to dismiss is to send away, and the following for says what replaces what is sent off

blocks.note: Andrew Strauss, a former England cricket captain
the opening letters of Australia
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An old England skipper gets Australia's opening batsmen out, piling pressure on the opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Strauss captained England at cricket and won the Ashes against Australia; swapping the AU in his name for E gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress and pressure are synonyms for strain, whether physical force on a material or mental tension.

clue.text: Rough characters cutting cocaine for piano lounge

indicators.note: cutting one thing for another means removing it and putting the other in its place

blocks.note: untidy handwriting, roughly formed letters
C is slang for cocaine
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: Rough types in a piano bar are cutting cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piano lounge' reads as a bar with a pianist; lounge is actually a verb here, and piano just gives P.
explanation.definitionFit: To sprawl is to lie or sit with limbs spread out lazily, which is to lounge.

clue.text: Binge dropping ecstasy periodically and space out

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it fall away, so a letter leaves the word before it
periodically means at regular intervals, so only every other letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: a bout of excessive indulgence
E is slang for the drug ecstasy
first and third letters of the word

explanation.surface: A clubber on a binge gives up ecstasy now and again and zones out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Space out' seems to mean being dazed from the drug, but it is the definition in its sense of arranging things apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To spread things is to distribute or extend them over an area, which is what spacing them out means.

clue.text: Partners right to bang inside - it's cleaner

indicators.note: something inside another sits within it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: West and East, partners at the bridge table
to strike
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Business partners vow to bang inside the premises and declare it a cleaner job.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, players sit as North, South, East and West, with West and East partnered, so partners can be WE.
explanation.definitionFit: Whiter is the comparative of white, and in washing-powder adverts the whiter wash is the cleaner one.

clue.text: Upset about limits to dud puzzle

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece wraps the other
the limits of a word are its two ends, so only its outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: to annoy or anger
first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone is annoyed by a puzzle that turns out to be a dud.
explanation.definitionFit: A riddle is a question or statement worded as a puzzle to be solved by guessing.

clue.text: One graphically capturing bull?

blocks.note: surface reading: an artist or photographer vividly depicting or catching a bull
setter's reading: a machine that records on a graph when someone talks bull, meaning nonsense or falsehood

explanation.surface: An artist vividly depicts a charging bull.
explanation.walkthrough: Bull is slang for nonsense or untruth, and the polygraph traces body responses as a graph, so it captures falsehood graphically.
explanation.definitionFit: A polygraph machine plots pulse and breathing on a chart to catch someone telling untruths.

clue.text: Takes in requirements of contract?

blocks.note: first meaning: deceives or fools
second meaning: in contract bridge, the number of card rounds a declarer must win

explanation.walkthrough: Contract is contract bridge, where the bid commits a player to win a set number of rounds, each one a trick.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means deceives, and in bridge it names the rounds of play a contract obliges declarer to win.

clue.text: Between pub and party regularly muse on suggestive remark

indicators.note: between puts the selected letters in the middle, flanked by the two words on either side
regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter of the phrase is taken

blocks.note: an inn is a pub
second, fourth and sixth letters of the two words
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Someone muses between pub and party over a cheeky comment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' looks like a link but it is part of the letters taken; muse on supplies U, E, N.
explanation.definitionFit: An innuendo is an indirect hint, usually smutty or disparaging, so it is a remark with a suggestion behind it.

clue.text: Barmy Army wanting maiden to go with new spinner's work

indicators.note: barmy means crazy, so the word after it is scrambled
wanting means lacking, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: England's cricket fans, the Barmy Army, react to a spin bowler's maiden over.
explanation.walkthrough: The Barmy Army are England's travelling cricket supporters; in cricket a maiden is an over with no runs and a spinner is a slow bowler, but here the spinner spins thread or tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarn is thread made by a spinner, and a spun yarn is also a tall story.

clue.text: Team push for something more enriching?

blocks.note: a side is a team
to push or jostle

explanation.surface: A coach drives the team on in search of more success.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on enriching: a second job literally makes you richer.
explanation.definitionFit: A side hustle is extra paid work alongside a main job, earning money that leaves you richer.

clue.text: Most secretive as this Lette cryptic

indicators.note: cryptic means obscure and coded, so the letters before it are disguised by rearranging

blocks.note: the eleven letters taken as written, including the setter's name

explanation.surface: The setter boasts that this very clue is as secretive as it gets.
explanation.walkthrough: Lette is the setter, and the name joins the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealthy means acting covertly to avoid notice, so the superlative is the most secretive.

clue.text: Ungrounded and deeply confused?

blocks.note: first meaning: afloat on the ocean, not on land
second meaning: bewildered and lost; deeply hints at the ocean's depths

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ungrounded' looks like baseless, but it means a ship not run aground; the question mark flags the play on deeply.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes being utterly bewildered, and literally describes a vessel afloat far from land.

clue.text: Unyielding Abbot discovered rule embraced by upright devotees

indicators.note: dis-covered means having its covering removed, so the word loses its outside letters
in a down entry, standing a word upright means reading it from bottom to top
being embraced by something means being held inside it

blocks.note: enthusiasts, as in fitness nuts
the word with its first and last letters stripped
R is the abbreviation for rule, as in Rex or regulation

explanation.surface: A stern abbot is found out breaking a rule his devout monks uphold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' is not found but dis-covered, the cover taken off; and 'upright' reads the devotees bottom to top in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stubborn refuses to give way or change their mind, which is being unyielding.

clue.text: Removing top, streak beside female and show off?

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the first letter, so it is taken off

blocks.note: a run of wins is a streak
F is the abbreviation for female
to air something is to show it publicly

explanation.surface: A streaker takes their top off beside a woman and shows off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show off' looks like a phrasal verb, but show gives AIR and off alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying behaviour is a bit off means it is unjust or not right, which is unfair.

clue.text: Set out both sides of defence strategy

indicators.note: the two sides of a word are its ends, so only its first and last letters are used

blocks.note: first and last letters
a ploy is a tactic or scheme

explanation.surface: A coach sets out a strategy for both flanks of the defence.
explanation.definitionFit: To deploy troops or resources is to position and arrange them ready for action.

clue.text: Largely dark and loveless election tragically crossed lines

indicators.note: largely means mostly but not all, so the word loses its final letter
love is zero in tennis scoring, so less love means losing an O
a tragic turn of events wrecks things, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; love is the letter O

explanation.surface: A grim, joyless election ends in a tragedy of crossed wires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crossed lines' suggests a misunderstanding, but it is the definition as a past-tense verb: threads woven over each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Interlaced means woven together so that strands pass over and under one another, crossing lines.

clue.text: Relaxation, for instance cuddling when home

indicators.note: to cuddle is to hug, so one piece wraps its arms around the others

blocks.note: e.g., short for exempli gratia, for example
as in 'as I left'
being in is being at home

explanation.surface: Relaxing means, say, cuddling up on the sofa once you're home.
explanation.definitionFit: Easing is the loosening of tension or restrictions, as in an easing of rules, which is a relaxation.

clue.text: Vilify European fellow assuming pantomime role

indicators.note: to assume is to take on, so one piece takes the others into it

blocks.note: the pantomime dame, a comic woman played by a man in British Christmas shows
E is the abbreviation for European
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A European man is mocked for taking the dame's part in panto.
explanation.walkthrough: Pantomime is a British family stage show at Christmas, whose stock comic dame is a man in drag.
explanation.definitionFit: To defame someone is to damage their good name with false claims, which is what vilifying does.

clue.text: Second-hand parts in warehouse displays

indicators.note: only parts of the words that follow are wanted, the letters running across them

blocks.note: the tail of the first word joined to the start of the second

explanation.surface: A warehouse shows off its second-hand parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Used goods have already belonged to someone else, which is what second-hand means.

clue.text: Raised voice in argument following shortfall?

indicators.note: something short is cut down, so the word attached to it loses its final letter
following puts the piece named before it second, after the piece named afterwards

blocks.note: read as two words, a fall made short by losing its last letter
a set-to is a quarrel

explanation.surface: Voices are raised in a row after money falls short.
explanation.walkthrough: Shortfall must be split: short fall gives FAL. 'Raised voice' sounds like shouting, but it is singing pitched high.
explanation.definitionFit: Falsetto is a male singer's artificially high register, a voice pitched above its natural range.

clue.text: Funny fabulist pulling good man's leg to a certain extent

indicators.note: funny means odd or peculiar, so the letters are put in a strange new order
pulling something out removes it, so letters are taken away

blocks.note: taken as written
a saint, abbreviated ST, is a good man

explanation.surface: A comic storyteller is pulling a good man's leg, up to a point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulling someone's leg' is teasing, but leg belongs to the definition, and pulling removes the saint.
explanation.definitionFit: The fibula is the outer bone of the lower leg, so it is only part of the leg.

clue.text: Scottish team taking last run out for spots of shooting practice

indicators.note: taking out means removing, and last says it is the final occurrence that goes

blocks.note: Rangers, the Glasgow football club
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A Scottish football side does target practice after a run.
explanation.walkthrough: Rangers is a Glasgow football club; RANGERS has two Rs and only the second goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Shooting ranges are the places where people practise firing at targets.

clue.text: S&M with men bound under orders for boot-licking

blocks.note: the letters as written
soldiers obliged to obey commands

explanation.surface: A sadomasochistic scene where men in bondage obey orders and lick boots.
explanation.walkthrough: The kinky surface makes boot-licking literal, but it is the definition for fawning.
explanation.definitionFit: Smarmy describes an oily, ingratiating manner, the flattery of someone sucking up to others.
